title: REST API design
subtitle: Nouns, methods, status codes and errors that clients can trust, and changes that never break an app already in use.

This story is made up, but the mistake is common. A web page updates on every reload. A mobile app on a phone may be months old. Your API must serve all of them.

You act on resources with a few standard HTTP methods: GET, POST, PUT, PATCH and DELETE. You do not invent a new URL for every action. Google's guide says APIs should prefer standard methods over custom ones.

An API is a promise to every client that uses it, including old ones you cannot update. Design it so you can add to it for years without breaking that promise.

Return 4xx for client mistakes and 5xx for server faults. Alerts on 5xx then mean real server problems.
Use one error format on every endpoint. Put a stable error
in it, so clients never parse the message text.
Write the OpenAPI file in the same
as the code. Review the file like code.
Plan deprecation: tell clients early, measure who still calls the old version, and remove it only when traffic is near zero.
"Write an OpenAPI spec for an orders API: create, get, list with cursor pagination, and update. Use RFC 9457 problem details for every error. Use camelCase field names."
"Compare this OpenAPI file with the version on main. List every change that could break an existing client, like a removed, renamed or retyped field."
"Add an Idempotency-Key header to POST /orders. Store the key with the order in one transaction, and reject a reused key with a different body."
Field names, casing and plural collection names are the same on every endpoint.
Every error uses the same problem details shape, with the right status code. No 200 with
POST endpoints that create things take an idempotency key. GET never changes data.
List endpoints are paginated, with a limit and a maximum page size.
Nothing was removed, renamed or made required compared with the last version. An agent may "tidy up" names, just like the developer in the story.
The status codes the code really returns match the ones in the OpenAPI file.

q.v: A client sends DELETE /orders/42 and the connection drops before the answer arrives. Is it safe to send it again?

options.v: No. DELETE is never safe to repeat.
Yes. DELETE is idempotent, so a second identical request has the same intended effect.
Only if the server returned 204 the first time.

why.v: RFC 9110 defines PUT, DELETE and the safe methods as idempotent. The answer may differ, but the effect is the same.

q.v: A new release of your API renames the field

options.v: break, because a rename is a remove plus an add.

why.v: Google's AIP-180 treats a rename like removing the old field, which breaks existing clients.

why.v: When data changes, the offset window moves. Slack saw skipped and repeated results and moved to cursors.

q.v: The request JSON is valid, but the quantity is -1. Which status code fits best?

why.v: RFC 9110 uses 422 when the syntax is correct but the server cannot process the instructions inside.

q.v: Why add pagination to a list endpoint in the first version, even if the list is small today?

options.v: Adding it later is a breaking change for existing clients.
It makes the database faster today.

why.v: Google AIP-158 and Microsoft's guidelines both say adding paging later breaks existing users.
